title: pH of a Weak Base
short: Solve Kb for [OH⁻], then change pOH to pH.
trouble: Students report the pOH as the pH, or use Ka where Kb is needed.

blocks.html: A weak base takes a proton from water and leaves $\mathrm{OH^-}$ behind. The calculation is the weak-acid one with $K_b$ in place of $K_a$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ in place of $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$, plus one last step from pOH to pH.

For $\mathrm{B + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HB^+ + OH^-}$: $K_b = \dfrac{x^2}{C - x}$ with $x = [\mathrm{OH^-}]$; often $x \approx \sqrt{K_bC}$. Then $\text{pOH} = -\log x$ and $\text{pH} = 14.00 - \text{pOH}$.

Ammonia and the amines have a lone pair on nitrogen that can accept a proton from water. Each base molecule that does so makes one $\mathrm{HB^+}$ and one $\mathrm{OH^-}$, so the ICE table is the same as for a weak acid. The equation gives $[\mathrm{OH^-}]$, not $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, so you get the pOH first.

blocks.title: A stronger weak base
steps: Shortcut: $x = \sqrt{(4.4 \times 10^{-4})(0.050)} = 4.7 \times 10^{-3}$, which is 9.4% of 0.050. Too big.

blocks.title: When only Ka is given
blocks.q: The table lists $K_a = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$ for $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$. What is $K_b$ for $\mathrm{NH_3}$?

blocks.title: A very weak base
steps: $\text{pOH} = 4.89$, so $\text{pH} = 9.11$: basic, but far less so than ammonia at the same concentration.

blocks.html: Anions of weak acids are weak bases too: acetate, fluoride and cyanide take protons from water. Their $K_b$ values are usually found from the acid's $K_a$, which is the next lesson's main tool. The weak-base calculation is then exactly the one above.
Reporting the pOH as the pH, or using $K_a$ where $K_b$ is needed. Check: any base gives a pH above 7. If your answer for a base is 2.78, you stopped at the pOH.
